steps.title: Can you feel a beat?
steps.text: Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel thump, thump, thump? That's a beat. Music has a beat too.

steps.intro: Stand up and march! Step on every beat. Try the tortoise, then the hare.

steps.title: Fizz is the drummer
steps.text: Fizz plays the drums: a big Boom, a snappy Tap and a tiny Tss.

wow.text: Super Mario Bros. came out in 1985. Its music used the hissy noise sound for the beat, just like Fizz.

steps.intro: {copilot}, tap the big drum with the beat!

steps.prompt: Listen. Is this tortoise speed or hare speed?
steps.reveal: Hare speed! The beat was fast. The speed of a beat can change: fast or slow.

steps.intro: Dance to the music. When it stops, freeze like a statue!

steps.title: The Speed Problem
steps.scenario: Moon Run needs music. Fast music is exciting, but it can feel rushed. Slow music is calm, but it can feel sleepy. How fast should our game's music be?

options.label: Slow, then faster near the flag

steps.reveal: Game makers have tried all three. In Space Invaders, from 1978, the music was just four notes, and it got faster as there were fewer aliens left. Other games keep the music calm so players can think.
steps.followUp: How does fast music make you feel? And slow music?

steps.intro: Make our game's beat! Tap boxes for Boom, Tap and Tss, then press Play. Change it until you love it.

steps.title: A pots-and-pans drum kit
need: A soft mat on the floor
steps: Turn the pots upside down on the mat.
Tap a beat together: boom, boom, boom, boom.
One of you plays a rhythm, the other copies it. Then try it soft, then loud!
steps.why: A beat stays steady like a heartbeat. A rhythm is the pattern you play on top of it.
steps.safety: Use light pans with no sharp edges, and stay close while spoons are flying.

debrief: What's your favourite speed to dance at?
Can you clap our game's beat?
